clue.text: One revealing a secret story of archery and apple?

blocks.note: William Tell, the Swiss marksman of legend, was made to shoot an apple off his own son's head with a crossbow
a tale is a story

explanation.surface: A quiz question about the old legend of the bowman and the fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The legend supplies one half and the plain word 'story' the other, but they arrive in the opposite order to the one the grid wants. The marksman was ordered to take the shot by a tyrannical Austrian governor.
explanation.definitionFit: A telltale is the one who runs off and reports what was meant to stay quiet — the schoolyard word for an informer.

clue.text: Not working to block part of golf-course? That’s sweet

indicators.note: To block a pipe or a path is to lodge yourself right inside it, so what has just been clued sits within what comes next.

blocks.note: the tee is the mown patch each hole is driven from
a machine that is not working is off

explanation.surface: An idler getting in the way on the golf course, and somebody calling that lovely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' is the British noun — a piece of confectionery — and not the adjective the surface is leaning on. Of a golf hole's parts, the tee is the one short enough for a setter to use.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a sweet is any piece of confectionery, and this boiled, buttery, jaw-sticking one has filled the shop jars for a century.

clue.text: Bet list of options getting reduced for ordinary fellows

indicators.note: Something reduced has been cut shorter, and a word cut shorter loses the letter at its end.

blocks.note: to lay a bet is to place one, the bookmaker's verb
a menu is a list of options, and shortened it drops its final U

explanation.surface: A betting shop trimming the choices on offer to its ordinary customers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bet' looks like a noun sitting next to 'list' and has to be read as a verb before it gives anything up. A menu need not be food — any list of choices is one.
explanation.definitionFit: A layman is anyone outside the clergy, or outside the profession under discussion, so the word means people with no special standing.

clue.text: Italian restaurant dessert overturned and a riot breaks out

indicators.note: Something overturned has been tipped up to stand the wrong way round, and in a down entry that means reading its letters upward.

blocks.note: a TART is a dessert, and stood on its head in a down entry it reads upward
the five letters of A RIOT in a new order

explanation.surface: A pudding knocked over in an Italian place and the room erupting into a brawl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overturned' means read upward because this is a down entry; across clues get 'recalled' or 'sent back' for the same job. Nine letters split four and five, with the definition doing no cryptic work at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A trattoria is the informal, family-run end of Italian eating out, plainer and cheaper than a ristorante.

clue.text: Sinister ambition as seen in US auto industry products?

definitions.note: The answer is a singular adjectival phrase and the definition a plural noun: the setter names it by what every car built for American roads is, with the question mark admitting the stretch.

blocks.note: sinister is the heraldic and Latin term for the left-hand side of a shield
drive is the push that gets someone to the top

explanation.surface: Something menacing about the ambitions of the American car makers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sinister' carries its old heraldic sense of the left side and the modern sense of menace is decoration. Britain drives on the left and puts the steering wheel on the right, so American cars are built the other way about.
explanation.definitionFit: Cars made for American roads carry the steering wheel on the left, so the phrase names the whole US output at a stroke.

clue.text: College grounds affected our group

blocks.note: camp means showily theatrical, affected in manner
the group the speaker belongs to is us

explanation.surface: A visit on which the college's land made an impression on the party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Affected' reads as a verb with 'our group' for its object, and it is an adjective meaning put-on or theatrical. Nothing in the clue moves or hides, so the only work is spotting that switch.
explanation.definitionFit: A campus is the land and buildings a college occupies, the American word that has taken over British universities too.

clue.text: High level to be attained in Greek?

blocks.note: the storey right up under the roof of a house
the dialect of ancient Athens, the Greek that Plato and Sophocles wrote

explanation.surface: A grade a student is hoping to reach in a Greek exam.
explanation.walkthrough: The dialect takes a capital A and the room under the roof does not, a difference no printed clue can show you. Everything between the two halves is there to hold the sentence together and nothing more.
explanation.definitionFit: An attic is the room immediately under the roof, the highest level of a house; Attic is also the Greek of ancient Athens, so the same five letters answer both.

clue.text: Left capital of Uruguay with girl, coming to European country

indicators.note: A capital letter is the big one a name starts with, so this takes the opening letter of the word that follows.

blocks.note: port is the left side of a ship as you face the bow
the capital letter Uruguay starts with, rather than Montevideo
gal is the informal spelling of girl

explanation.surface: Someone leaving the Uruguayan capital with a young woman and heading for Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital of' baits the solver into hunting for Montevideo when it wants a single capital letter. 'Left' is the nautical side rather than the political wing, and the two misdirections sit in the same three words.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition names a class and leaves you to supply a member of it: Portugal is the country along the western edge of Iberia.

clue.text: Watch indecent tapes etc.

indicators.note: Indecent means not decent, and letters that refuse to behave decently will not stay in the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: Settling down to view a stash of dirty videos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Etc.' almost never earns its letters in a clue, and here all three of them are working. 'Indecent' looks like a description of the tapes and is the instruction instead.
explanation.definitionFit: To spectate is to be a spectator — to look on at a game or an incident without taking any part in it.

clue.text: Rugby player with three legs?

blocks.note: the number 10, who stands off behind the scrum half and decides what the backs do next
the position's name read as an arithmetic: an insect walks on six legs, so half of one is down to three

explanation.surface: A rugby player who has somehow grown an extra leg.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here comes apart into letters. The position's name is two words, and the second is read as a fraction taken of the creature the first names.
explanation.definitionFit: The fly half wears 10 and stands off from the scrum, and the two words also read as a quantity of insect legs — six halved.

clue.text: OAP, perhaps, regarding one in tree

indicators.note: What is in a thing sits inside it, so the letter just named is planted within the word that follows.

blocks.note: re means regarding, the heading at the top of a memo
the word tree supplies its own four letters
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A pensioner's opinion of somebody who has climbed up a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: OAP is the British label for an old age pensioner, the person drawing the state pension. 'Perhaps' is the setter's flag that the definition offers an instance rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A retiree is anyone who has left work for good, and a British old age pensioner is one familiar instance of that.

clue.text: Senior cleric correct to turn back almost before conclusion

indicators.note: Almost a word is the word all but finished, so its last letter never arrives.

blocks.note: right means correct
to revert is to turn back, and stopping almost at the end of it loses the T
a conclusion is an end, and the rest of the wordplay comes before it

explanation.surface: An instruction to change your mind just short of the finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn back' looks like a reversal instruction and is a straight synonym for a verb. The Right Reverend is how a bishop is styled in Britain, on envelopes and in orders of service.
explanation.definitionFit: The Right Reverend is the formal style of a bishop, so the definition names the rank by the title that goes in front of it.

clue.text: Still time for an occasion

blocks.note: the two are interchangeable intensifiers — still better, even better
t = time, the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: There being just enough time left to fit something in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' reads as 'yet' in the sentence and works as the intensifier sense instead, the one that means 'even'. A single abbreviated letter tacked on the end is the commonest shape in the puzzle, and 'time' is its commonest source.
explanation.definitionFit: An event is something that happens at an appointed time — a sports day, a wedding, an occasion marked in the diary.

clue.text: Royal Household drugged? That’s where judges will be needed

definitions.note: The definition describes the answer by what goes on in it rather than offering a noun that could be swapped straight in.

blocks.note: someone high is under the effect of a drug
the court is the monarch's household, attendants and all

explanation.surface: A suggestion that the palace staff have been at something they shouldn't.
explanation.walkthrough: The court is the royal one in the wordplay and the judicial one in the answer, which is the joke the clue is built on. The High Court of England and Wales hears the most serious civil cases.
explanation.definitionFit: The High Court is the senior civil court of England and Wales, staffed by judges rather than magistrates, so it is named here by who has to sit in it.

clue.text: Stop – when the pepper runs out?

definitions.text: Stop – when the pepper runs out?

blocks.note: the plain sense: to slow down and come to a standstill, said of an engine, a car or a project
a mill with nothing left in it has no more work to do, so the turning is over

explanation.surface: A pepper mill being twisted round and round with nothing left inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for coming slowly to a standstill happens to contain the very verb a pepper mill performs, and that collision is the whole clue. No part of it breaks down into letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To grind to a halt is to slow to a stop, and the machinery-seizing-up picture behind the idiom is exactly what an empty mill does.

clue.text: Vegetable lorry that guy brought round OK

indicators.note: To bring something round is to carry it about the outside of a thing, so the letters just named close over what follows.

blocks.note: an artic is British for an articulated lorry, the tractor-and-trailer rig that hauls freight down the motorway
the pronoun for the man already mentioned
the two letters are simply written into the clue

explanation.surface: A man delivering a lorryload of vegetables without any trouble at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'OK' sits in the sentence looking like a comment on how the delivery went, and it is two letters to be swallowed. The everyday clipping of 'articulated' is what makes the long opening chunk possible.
explanation.definitionFit: The artichoke is either the thistle-like head eaten leaf by leaf or the knobbly Jerusalem tuber, and both are vegetables.

clue.text: Initially locked in lavatory – situation displayed in online comment

indicators.note: Initially means at the very start, so only the opening letter of the word it introduces is taken.
In is the plainest container word there is: whatever is in a thing sits inside it.

blocks.note: bog is British slang for a lavatory
the opening letter of LOCKED
a post is a job or situation, as in the situations vacant column

explanation.surface: Getting shut in the toilet and then telling the internet all about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Situation' is the old word for a job — 'situations vacant' still heads the small ads — and that is the sense wanted. The dash carries no instruction; it only lets two unrelated halves share a sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A blog post is one dated entry on a personal website, a single person's comment published online.

clue.text: Wealthy area heading off industrial waste

indicators.note: A word's heading is the letter standing at its head, and heading it off takes that letter away.

blocks.note: a = area, the standard abbreviation
effluent is the liquid waste a factory pours out, and its opening E is removed

explanation.surface: A rich district getting rid of the filth the factories have produced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heading off' reads as chasing something away, which is just what a wealthy district does with its waste, and the instruction is meant literally instead. Effluent and affluent differ by a letter and share the Latin fluere, to flow.
explanation.definitionFit: Affluent means having money in abundance — the word an estate agent reaches for when 'rich' sounds too blunt.

clue.text: Long sentence with full stop? It’s critical

blocks.note: life is the longest sentence a British court can hand down
'with' joins two things together and so does 'and'
the full stop after which nothing at all follows

explanation.surface: A grammarian complaining about an over-long sentence that finally reaches its full stop.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all punctuation and the wordplay is all courtroom. 'With' quietly earning three letters of its own is the piece most solvers walk straight past.
explanation.definitionFit: A life-and-death matter is one where everything turns on the outcome, which is what calling something critical says.

clue.text: Felt sad for coalmine that is dead

blocks.note: the pit is what every British mining town calls its colliery
ie is short for the Latin id est, that is
d = dead, the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Mourning a colliery that has closed for good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That is' is the reliable signal for those two Latin letters, and it hides easily inside a sentence about a mine. Britain's pit villages lost their collieries in the 1980s, which is the scene the surface leans on.
explanation.definitionFit: To pity someone is to feel sorrow on their behalf, and the past tense of it matches the definition's.

clue.text: Magazine number showing quantity of champagne

blocks.note: mag is the everyday short form of magazine
num is the standard shortening of number, as printed on a form

explanation.surface: The issue number printed on the cover of a periodical.
explanation.walkthrough: Two shortenings run together with nothing to mark either of them, which is what makes a six-letter charade harder than its length suggests. A magnum holds 1.5 litres, exactly two ordinary bottles.
explanation.definitionFit: A magnum is the double-sized bottle rather than a synonym for champagne, so the definition names it by the measure it holds.

clue.text: Explosive set to catch fire

blocks.note: to gel is to set, the way a jelly firms up in the fridge
to ignite is to catch fire

explanation.surface: A charge laid and left ready to go up in flames.
explanation.walkthrough: The sentence could be describing the answer from end to end, which is why the seam between definition and wordplay is so hard to find. 'Set' is the verb of jellies here, not of laying a charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Gelignite is the nitroglycerine-based blasting explosive used in quarries and much loved by fictional safe-crackers.

clue.text: Assess Georgia – not initially vast

indicators.note: Not initially says the word is all there except at its beginning, so its first letter goes.

blocks.note: GA is the postal code for the American state of Georgia
huge is vast, and without its initial H that is what is left

explanation.surface: Sizing up Georgia, a place not enormous to begin with.
explanation.walkthrough: Georgia is both an American state and a country in the Caucasus, and only the state carries a two-letter code. The dash is the seam: everything after it is one word with its head cut off.
explanation.definitionFit: To gauge something is to measure or estimate it — you gauge a mood, a distance or a crowd, which is assessing it.

clue.text: Church in America or another country

blocks.note: ch = church, as printed on an Ordnance Survey map
the word in supplies its own two letters
a = America, the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A church somewhere in the States, or else one abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like the word joining two pieces and turns out to be a piece itself, handing over both its letters. 'Another' does nothing but rule out the country already named in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition names a class and leaves the member to be found: China is a country, and 'another' only excludes the America standing next to it.

clue.text: Excessively quote old poetry about Unionist

indicators.note: To be about something is to be all the way around it, so the letters just clued open up and take the next one inside.

blocks.note: o = old, the standard abbreviation
verse is poetry
u = Unionist, from the parties that carry the word in Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: Somebody quoting far too much old poetry on the subject of a Unionist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' has to be read as the container instruction rather than the harmless 'on the subject of' the sentence offers. The single letter it swallows sits inside a five-letter word, leaving an uneven split.
explanation.definitionFit: To overuse something is to wheel it out more often than it will bear, which is what quoting a line excessively does to it.

clue.text: Recalled uproar about limits to our coastal decline?

definitions.note: Erosion is any wearing away and not only the sea's, so the question mark flags a definition by one familiar example.

indicators.note: To recall something is to call it back, and letters called back arrive in the reverse of the order they left in.
Something set about a thing is wrapped around its outside, so these letters take the next ones within them.
The limits of a word are the points at which it stops, which are its first and its last letter.

blocks.note: noise is uproar, din
the outermost letters of OUR

explanation.surface: A remembered row about how far our shoreline has worn back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recalled' governs the whole of the wordplay and not just the word beside it, so the insertion is made first and the turnaround comes last. 'Our' is not a possessive at all but a three-letter word to be stripped.
explanation.definitionFit: Erosion is the slow wearing away of land by sea and weather, so a coastline steadily losing ground is the sense the clue points at.

clue.text: What helps to regulate the Rottweiler?

definitions.text: What helps to regulate the Rottweiler?

blocks.note: the letters run on from the end of REGULATE through THE and into the start of ROTTWEILER

explanation.surface: Asking what it takes to keep a big dog under control.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no hidden-word signal anywhere; the question mark is the only hint that the sentence is doing two jobs at once. Letters that straddle three words are the hardest sort to catch.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: a tether is the rope or chain that fastens an animal to a fixed point, which is what keeps a Rottweiler where you want it.

clue.text: Man and dude confused about Democrat’s extra comment

indicators.note: Something confused is muddled and out of order, so the letters it describes cannot be trusted in the sequence given.
Set about a thing means wrapped around it, so the muddled letters close over the one named next.

blocks.note: the seven letters of MAN and DUDE in a new order
d = Democrat, as used throughout American election coverage

explanation.surface: Two blokes getting muddled up over something a Democrat has said.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s reads as a possessive and is only there to join, and the letter it hands over goes inside the jumble rather than after it. 'Man and dude' is an odd pairing to write, which is usually the sign of fodder chosen for its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An addendum is the bit added at the end of a book or a report, a further remark tacked on once the main text is done.
